1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: French Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.background: The position was seen as so normal that no one thought of claiming a name for it.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5.strategy: Attacks the f6 knight with a pawn, gaining space and a tempo, and locks the centre. White gets room and kingside prospects; Black must undermine the pawn chain from its base, and its knight has to retreat, losing time.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.name: French Defence, Classical, 4. Bg5
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6 knight against the queen, so that e5 becomes a real threat, and asks Black how it will deal with that. It is the classical main line: White develops with tempo, and Black must choose between solid defence and counterattack.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.exd5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Delayed Exchange Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.exd5.strategy: Releases the central tension and heads for a simple, quiet game. White trades its space advantage for safety, and Black has an easy time developing with no weaknesses to worry about.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bd3.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the options open, but the bishop blocks the queen's defence of d4 and gives Black an easy game: ...dxe4 and a trade of knights relieve the position at once.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Be3.name: French Defence: Henneberger Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Be3.strategy: Supports d4 and prepares queenside castling, but it is a slow, modest move: the f6 knight is not attacked and Black can develop freely or take on e4 whenever it likes.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Normal Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7.background: The line 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5 Nfd7 6.Bxe7 Qxe7 used to be the main line of the French Defence; the Burn Variation (4...dxe4) has since overtaken 4...Be7 in popularity.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7.strategy: The classical way to meet the pin: the bishop interposes, so the f6 knight no longer hangs on the queen and can retreat if e5 comes. Black accepts a little less space for a sound structure and a plan of striking back at the centre with ...c5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Burn Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4.background: Named after Amos Burn. It is the most common reply to 4.Bg5 at the top level and has long been a favourite of Evgeny Bareev.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn before White can push it, so e5 is no longer a threat. After the recapture White's pieces are active, but Black has a solid game, often with the bishop pair, and strikes back at the centre with ...c5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4.background: Named after John Lindsay McCutcheon, a lawyer from Pennsylvania, who brought it to public attention by beating World Champion Wilhelm Steinitz with it in a simultaneous exhibition in New York in 1885. It was most popular from 1905 until 1925 and was revived in 1990.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4.strategy: Counterattacks instead of unpinning: the bishop pins the knight on c3, so that White's e5 can be met by hitting the bishop on g5. It is the sharpest answer to the pin, a tactical game in which Black often gives up the bishop for the knight and accepts weakened dark squares near its king.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Attacks the pinned knight with a pawn and gains space, the principled reply to the counterattack. White accepts a sharp game: the bishop on g5 becomes a target, and Black has a direct way to challenge it.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.ex.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Exchange Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.ex.strategy: Resolves the tension instead of pushing e5, and keeps the pin on f6. Black cannot retake with the knight, because the bishop on g5 would then take the queen, so it needs another recapture. A less ambitious way to meet the counterattack that gives up the space gained by e5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.Ne.strategy: Prepares a3, so that a trade on c3 is retaken by the knight and White's pawns stay whole. It offers the e4 pawn in return for development, and the pin on f6 is the compensation; playable but it gives Black a free pawn to start with.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Counterattacks the bishop at once. Both sides now have a piece under fire: Black's knight is attacked by the e5 pawn, White's bishop by the h-pawn, and White must choose between retreating and carrying out the threat.

Trades the bishop for the knight with check, but the knight on f6 is still attacked and pinned to the queen, so ...h6 is still needed. White's doubled pawns are small compensation: Black has lost the dark-squared bishop and the kingside is left exposed.

Retreats the attacked knight and uncovers the queen: Bxd8 wins it, and Black's recaptures on c3 and d8 repay only a knight and a bishop for it. The knight has to be saved with a counterattack on the bishop instead.

The main line: the bishop retreats to a protected square and now guards the knight on c3. Black usually trades on c3 and the knight escapes to e4; White gets the bishop pair and a strong pawn centre, Black a damaged queenside to attack.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Chigorin Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Carries out the threat at once: Black takes the bishop, and the pawn captures on g7, where it attacks the rook. The result is a sharp trade of knight for bishop that leaves Black's kingside pawns splintered but opens lines for its rooks.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Bernstein Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Keeps the pin alive: the knight is attacked by the pawn and the bishop, and Black must act. The bishop stays exposed to ...g5, which weakens Black's kingside but also forces White to retreat again, so White gains little for the tempo.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Dr. Olland Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Retreats all the way home: the bishop is safe, but the trip has cost two moves, and the knight on c3 stays pinned against the king while Black's knight escapes the e5 pawn with time to spare.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Janowski Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Retreats to e3, where the bishop protects d4 and cannot be hit by a knight on e4 as it could on d2. The knight on c3 stays pinned against the king, though, and White gains little: Black trades on c3 and the knight comes to e4 anyway.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Lasker Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight before a3 can force the issue. If White retakes with the b-pawn, White is left with doubled c-pawns, and Black's knight gets the e4 square. The price is the bishop pair and the dark squares, and White's big pawn centre gives White the initiative.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Tartakower Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5.strategy: Retreats the attacked knight but keeps the bishop on b4, so the tension stays and Black can still choose when to trade. The cost is time and space: the e5 pawn cramps Black, the knight shuts in the c8 bishop, and a3 forces the bishop to decide anyway.

Looks like a double attack on the bishop and knight, but White just takes the knight: after ...Bxd2+ the knight on e4 recaptures on d2, and Black is a piece down. The knight lunge loses material outright.

Recaptures the bishop with the pawn, so material stays level, and the h-file is half-open for Black's rook. White's pawn on f6 is a thorn, but if it takes on g7, the rook swings to g8 and Black wins the pawn back.

Takes the knight with check before recapturing on g5, which doubles White's c-pawns. But it gives up the dark-squared bishop that guards the kingside, and after bxc3 hxg5 fxg7 the pawn that lands on g7 gives White a lasting initiative against the king.
Retakes the pawn instead of the bishop, but the knight is already lost: the bishop simply retreats to h4 or d2 and White is a piece up for a pawn.
Retakes with the queen, which the bishop on g5 captures: Bxf6 wins the queen for a bishop and Black is far behind in material.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.ex.strategy: Recaptures with the queen because 5...Nxd5 would leave the queen on d8 hanging to the bishop on g5. The queen centralises and attacks that bishop in turn, forcing White to act at once, and White's best answer takes the knight on f6 to damage Black's kingside pawns.

Retakes with the pawn and heads for a symmetrical centre. White can trade the pinning bishop for the knight at once, Bxf6 Qxf6, and the position is level and quiet, with Black having to play for activity rather than for an edge.
Retakes with the knight, which unmasks the bishop on g5: Bxd8 wins the queen, and what Black wins back on c3 and d8 is worth much less than a queen.

The bishop is attacked by the queen, so it takes the knight first. Black can only recapture with the g-pawn, which leaves doubled f-pawns and an isolated h-pawn. White gives up the bishop pair for that, so White has to show the damaged pawns are worth more than Black's active pieces.

Retreats with a threat: the bishop unpins the knight on c3, which now attacks the queen. White keeps the bishop pair after a trade on c3, but gives up the chance to damage Black's structure and the game becomes level.

A quiet retreat that guards d4 and keeps the bishop, but it concedes that the pin on f6 has achieved nothing. The knight on c3 stays pinned, and Black develops freely with no weaknesses to worry about.

The only recapture, since the queen cannot reach f6. Black accepts doubled f-pawns and an isolated h-pawn, but gets the bishop pair, a half-open g-file and a centralised queen. White plays for a lasting pawn weakness, Black for piece activity.
Takes the knight with check before recapturing on f6, so bxc3 doubles White's c-pawns. Black still has to retake with the g-pawn, and gives up the bishop pair that makes the damaged f-pawns bearable.
Checks first instead of recapturing, but gains nothing: White blocks with a developing move and the g-pawn still has to retake on f6, doubling Black's pawns, often with the queens traded.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Pushes the pawn with a gain of time, since it attacks the knight and so answers the unpinning with a threat of its own. White commits to a cramping pawn chain and a space advantage, and Black must find counterplay against the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.Bx.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Richter Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.Bx.strategy: Takes the knight that attacks e4, so the pawn can stay where it is. White gives up the bishop pair, and Black recaptures with a bishop that eyes d4. White plays for a solid centre rather than a cramping pawn chain.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.ex.strategy: Releases the central tension and steers for a symmetrical pawn structure. White gives up any space edge, and Black develops without problems: a quiet game with little for either side.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.Bx.strategy: The natural recapture: Black keeps healthy pawns and the bishop pair, and the bishop on f6 eyes the d4 pawn along the long diagonal. Taking with the g-pawn would hand White a lasting target on the kingside.
Recaptures with the pawn, which doubles the f-pawns, weakens the kingside and blocks the diagonal of the bishop on e7. Black gets no activity in return for the damaged structure.
Grabs a pawn before recapturing: White takes on e7, Black's queen takes back, and Nxe4 then wins the pawn again. White ends a whole piece up for nothing.

Gains space and drives the bishop back, but it costs White time and fixes the pawn on e5, where Black can attack it from both sides while keeping the bishop pair. The bishop has to retreat, since taking on e5 only loses a piece to the d-pawn. Playable, but it gives Black an easy game.

Develops a piece and guards d4 against the bishop on f6, keeping the centre flexible. White has given up the bishop pair but keeps the space, and the game stays balanced, with Black's two bishops providing the counterplay.
Resolves the tension in the centre by exchanging pawns and heads for a symmetrical structure. That removes White's chance of an edge: Black keeps the bishop pair and develops freely.
Retreats the attacked bishop and keeps it, so Black holds the bishop pair. The e5 pawn cramps Black, but the structure is solid and Black has natural ways to attack the pawn chain and free the game.
Takes the pawn with the bishop, but the pawn is guarded by the d-pawn: dxe5 wins the bishop for a pawn and Black has nothing to show for it.
Keeps the bishop, but on an exposed square: White develops with a gain of time, since Nf3 attacks it. Black has the bishop pair for a little longer and has lost a move for it.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: The main retreat: the knight leaves the attacked square for one from which it hits the e5 pawn and helps to undermine the chain. The cost is a cramped position with the c8 bishop shut in, but Black has a firm structure and a clear plan against the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Tartakower Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Counterattacks the c3 knight and offers exchanges to ease the cramp. If the pieces come off, White's queen can swing to g4, hitting the e4 pawn and g7 at once, so Black has to defend accurately. It frees the game at the price of a pawn on e4 that is hard to hold.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Vistaneckis Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Takes the knight all the way home, losing two tempi for a modest idea: to recapture on e7 with the knight if the bishops are traded. White simply keeps the bishop and enjoys the extra space and a big lead in development.

Trades the dark-squared bishops now that Black's bishop attacks the one on g5, and leaves the e5 pawn cramping Black. White keeps the space advantage and builds a broad pawn centre; Black has a solid but passive position and plays for a counter-strike against the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.background: A gambit devised by Adolf Albin and played by Chatard, it was not taken seriously until Alekhine's game against Fahrni at Mannheim in 1914.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: A pawn gambit: the h-pawn protects the bishop on g5, so if Black trades, the h-file opens for a kingside attack on a king that struggles to find a safe place. Black's natural ...c5 break runs into a knight jump to b5. Sharp and risky, with an attack instead of a space advantage.

Declines the trade and keeps the bishop, which now backs up the e5 pawn from f4. White holds the space and denies the cramped side the exchange that would ease its game, but no longer pressures e7, and Black's play against the chain goes ahead unhindered.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.background: It used to be the main line of the French Defence, but the Burn Variation has since overtaken 4...Be7 in popularity, and 6.h4 now rivals 6.Bxe7 in frequency.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen and keeps the right to castle; a king recapture would give it up for no reason. Black has given up the dark-squared bishop, so the cramped position needs a pawn break to free it, while White has the space.
Recaptures with the king, which gives up castling for no reason and leaves it in front of the cramping pawn on e5. Black has to find counterplay with the king stuck in the centre.
Takes the pawn but leaves the queen on d8, which the bishop on e7 attacks: Bxd8 wins it for a bishop at best. Black has to recapture on e7 first.

Accepts the gambit: after the bishops are traded, Black's queen takes the g5 pawn and Black is a pawn up. The price is time and king safety, because White's pieces swing to the kingside while Black's king has no safe home.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Maróczy Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Declines the pawn and takes b5 from White's knight, but it loses time to the attack. Qg4 threatens Bxe7 and then Qxg7, so Black has to take on g5 and open the h-file; the kings are unsafe and White keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Breyer Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Strikes at d4 in the way Black normally meets this structure, but here it is too slow: the bishops come off and a knight lands on b5, threatening a fork on c7 and a check on d6. Black has to spend time on that, with the king under pressure from the advanced h-pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Spielmann Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Castles into the attack: with the h-pawn already advanced, Bd3 aims at h7 and the queen can follow to h5. This is the king position the gambit was built to attack, and White is clearly better.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Teichmann Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once but opens the e8-h5 diagonal: Qh5+ g6 exf6 leaves the king without cover. Black removes the cramping pawn at too high a price, and White is clearly ahead.

Declines the gambit and asks the bishop at once. After the bishops come off with Bxe7 Qxe7, Black has a sound game and the king is not yet committed, though White goes on to attack the kingside with a pawn storm.

Avoids the trade that the knight's retreat was aiming for and keeps the bishop on a good diagonal that also protects d4. White keeps the extra space and the lead in development, and Black's retreat has cost time.

Keeps the bishop out of the trade on a diagonal that guards e5, and White holds the space and the lead in development. Unlike Be3 it leaves d4 with little support, so ...c5 comes at once and White's edge shrinks to about a quarter of a pawn.
Trades the dark-squared bishops, but the knight can recapture on e7, a good square, so Black's retreat pays off. White keeps the space edge, though the cramped side is glad of the exchange.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Frankfurt Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Prepares to trade off the light-squared bishop, the French's problem piece, on the a6 diagonal. But after the knight's detour Black is far behind in development, and White holds the centre with ease.
Develops with pressure on d4 and e5, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so ...c5, the natural strike at the chain, is held up. White simply develops and keeps a clearer edge than after 6...c5.

Strikes at the base of the chain at once, the usual French way. White can take on c5, where the bishop on e3 guards the pawn, but Black has pieces ready to attack it and gets open lines in return. White keeps more space and the lead in development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Recaptures the pawn with a knight that now eyes f6 together with the bishop on g5. White has regained the pawn and has an open centre, and Black has to decide how to defend the knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.B.strategy: Trades the bishop for the pinned knight at once and wins the e4 pawn back afterwards. A safe and simple game, but White gives up the bishop and has little of the opening initiative left.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.f.strategy: A pawn gambit: White leaves e4 and plays f3 to open the f-file and keep the pin. Taking on f3 wins a pawn, but White's lead in development is nearly worth it; the simple recapture on e4 is no worse and less risky.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.name: French Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.background: The main line of the Burn Variation, long a favourite of Evgeny Bareev.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Ends the pin by blocking the line to the queen, and adds a second defender to the f6 knight, so it is comfortably defended. Black has given up the centre pawn for quick development and a solid position.
Defends the pinned knight with the other knight, so that an exchange on f6 can be met with a piece recapture. Black stays solid and keeps the bishop flexible, at the cost of hemming in the c8 bishop.
Takes the knight, but the f6 knight was the only piece shielding the queen from the bishop on g5: Bxd8 wins the queen. The check on b4 that follows does not make up for it.
Trades the bishop for the knight and accepts the loss of the bishop pair. White keeps the active knight on e4 and a space edge; Black has the bishop pair and dynamic chances.

Trades the knight for the attacker of e4 and, after the recapture and the bishop trade, simplifies the position. A safe and level game, but White has traded away most of the tension and the knight's active post.
Pulls the attacked knight back instead of trading it. It avoids simplification and keeps the pieces on, but the retreat costs time, which Black uses to complete its development.

The main recapture: Black keeps a sound pawn structure and the bishop pair, and the bishop looks down the long diagonal towards d4. Black has to develop and trade pieces carefully, because White has the freer centre and the active knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Burn Variation, Morozevich Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.background: Played by Alexander Morozevich and Gregory Kaidanov.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn instead: Black accepts doubled f-pawns for a half-open g-file and active pieces, and the pawn can advance to kick the knight from e4. Black gets piece activity at the price of a damaged structure.
Grabs the d4 pawn with the queen, but the queen on d1 guards it: Qxd4 simply wins Black's queen. The recapture on f6 has to come first.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7.strategy: Retreats the attacked knight to the square that keeps it in play: from d7 it hits the e5 pawn and prepares a break against the chain. Black gives up space and shuts in the c8 bishop for a solid structure and a clear plan against d4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Ne4.strategy: Counters instead of retreating and trades the knight for White's. But recapturing with the d-pawn doubles Black's e-pawns and gives up the centre, so the e4 pawn becomes a target while White's centre stays intact.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Ng8.strategy: Retreats all the way home, which costs a second tempo with the same knight. White gets a big lead in development and a cramping pawn on e5 for free, and Black is left with passive play.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.strategy: Defends the e5 pawn and takes a big space advantage. White commits the kingside to the pawn chain and loosens the e3 square and the king's diagonal. Black has a clear target in the base of the chain at d4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.Nc.name: French Defence: Classical Variation, Shirov-Anand Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.Nc.strategy: Reroutes the knight so that both the c-pawn and the f-pawn can advance to support the centre, while the knight guards d4 and the f4 square. It is a slower, solid set-up that gives up the knight's pressure on d5 and e4 and lags in development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.Qg.name: French Defence: Steinitz Variation, Gledhill Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.Qg.strategy: An early queen sortie that hits g7 and e6, but both are guarded, so it makes no real threat. It spends a tempo and gives Black time to strike at the d4 pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.strategy: Undermines the base of the pawn chain at once: if d4 falls, the e5 pawn loses its support and the knight takes it. White has to keep defending d4, which slows the rest of White's development.
Develops and prepares castling, but does nothing yet about the pawn chain. White has a free move to strengthen d4 and e5 and finish development before Black can challenge the centre.

Adds a piece against d4 and e5 but plugs the c-pawn's path, so the natural break against the base of the chain is gone. Black must find another way to challenge the centre while White finishes development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.name: French Defence: Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.background: 6.Nf3 is part of the main line of the Steinitz Variation: 5.f4 c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.Be3.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.strategy: Develops and defends both d4 and e5, so the chain holds. White keeps the space and a solid centre, and Black piles up pressure on d4 and e5 with pieces.

Takes a pawn it cannot keep: Black's knight and bishop both attack c5 and nothing defends it. The capture also gives up the d4 pawn, the base of White's chain, so e5 is left with just the f-pawn behind it. Black regains the pawn and the initiative.

Defends d4 a second time with the queen's knight and clears the c-pawn to support the centre. The price is that the knight leaves its active post, gives up the pressure on d5 and blocks the king's bishop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.name: French Defence: Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4.strategy: Puts the e5 pawn under double attack before regaining the c5 pawn, which White cannot hold. White must first deal with the threat to the centre, and Black gets the lead in development.
Regains the pawn at once with a developing move and keeps the e5 pawn under pressure from the knight. White's chain has lost its d4 base, so e5 is held only by the f-pawn, and Black has an easy game.
Regains the pawn with the d7 knight, but that takes the pressure off the e5 pawn, and the knight on c5 can be chased by b4. Black has the pawn back and White has time to consolidate.
Adds a second attacker to d4 and to e5, so both centre pawns are under pressure. Black keeps the tension, and White has to keep its pawn chain protected while it completes its development.
Takes on d4 at once, so White must recapture with a piece. Black keeps its pieces active and the e5 pawn under pressure, but gives White the open centre and a knight on d4.
Develops and prepares castling, but adds nothing to the pressure on d4 and e5. White is free to settle the centre, and Black has given up the initiative.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.exd5 exd5.strategy: Recaptures and reaches a symmetrical pawn structure where Black has no problems: the c8 bishop is free now that the e6 pawn is gone, and neither side has a weakness. A quiet game with equality likely, and little for either side unless someone errs.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.exd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight and keeps the e-pawn on e6. The knight is exposed in the centre to the knight on c3, and White can trade it off at once, after which Black has gained nothing over the pawn recapture.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Hangs the queen: the knight on c3 attacks d5, and Nxd5 wins the queen for a knight.
